title: Curb Verdict
pitch: A pole of stacked parking plates stands on an invented street, a stone gargoyle perched on top, and the visitor must rule on each case: may this car, with this permit, at this day and hour, stay, and until when? Behind the jokes is a real rules engine that merges time windows, day masks, permits and street-cleaning slots into a week-long legality strip, so every wrong answer shows exactly which plate decided it. A second mode, Sign Smith, hands you a target pattern and a plate budget and scores how few plates reproduce it.
whyNow: Timeless. Rescues a universally groaned-at subject (parking rules) by turning rule-reading into a deduction puzzle with a deadpan gargoyle judge.

research.summary: Search results show confusing stacked parking signs are a recurring complaint in several countries, and that phone apps now read photographed signs, yet no game or quiz about decoding them turned up. Reading guides describe layered plates of days, time windows, permit exceptions, street-cleaning slots and arrows. The page will use an invented municipal code and invented sign vocabulary (no real jurisdiction, no real signage), so the engine is fully specified by the page itself and the real-world sources only establish that the pain and the gap are real.

facts.claim: As of 2026-10-10, news reports from the UK (ITV, 2024-12-04) and US cities (Washington DC, Chicago) describe drivers and officials struggling with confusing parking signs.
As of 2026-10-10, search found phone apps that decode photographed parking signs (a Montreal team's app, Parky.AI) but no game or quiz built around decoding them.
Reported by one guide, unconfirmed: stacked plates are read top to bottom, with day plates, time windows and permit wording each changing the answer.
Reported by one catalog entry, unconfirmed: a 2009 New York user study found existing signs mismatched drivers' mental models.

inspirations: gargoyle judge on a cathedral roof

design.coreLoop: Each case shows a pole, a car with a permit type, and a day and time. The visitor chooses stay or leave and then the latest legal departure time on a week strip. The engine reveals the deciding plate and the full legality timeline, and the gargoyle comments. Cases escalate from one plate to six, with generated traps (exception plates, overnight windows that wrap midnight, cleaning slots that bite only on one weekday) so minute ten feels different from minute one. Sign Smith mode inverts it: build a stack to match a target legality pattern with the fewest plates.
sophisticationHooks: Rules engine: each plate is {action, day mask, minute window (may wrap midnight), permit exceptions, limit}; the week is 10080 minutes, rules are compiled into merged intervals, and precedence is the most restrictive active plate, with an explain trace naming the deciding plate
Seeded case generator (mulberry32 from the date or a hash seed) that uses the solver to guarantee a unique answer and a difficulty score based on how often the naive top-plate reading is wrong
Sign Smith inverse mode: a small search (greedy plus bounded brute force over plate templates) computes the minimum plate count, so the visitor's score is relative to the optimum
Week legality strip and explain overlay that make the logic visible; shareable URL hash holds seed, mode and answers
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: pure rules module (compile, evaluate, explain, generate, solve), SVG pole and gargoyle art drawn by hand, Verdict mode with about 40 generated cases per seed, Sign Smith mode with 12 target patterns, share link, about/making-of panel, light/dark, reduced motion, keyboard play. Cut: multiple cities, real signage, sound beyond one soft stamp sound, accounts, streak sync.
risks: Must use an invented jurisdiction and invented plate styling; no real sign designs, no legal advice, with a visible note that the in-game code is fictional
Rule-precedence ambiguity could make answers feel unfair; mitigated by printing the in-game municipal code and showing the explain trace
Reported guide specifics and the 2009 study remain unverified, so the page cites them only as 'as of 2026-10-10, per <source>' or omits them
